patient_answer: Rest completely and maintain aggressive oral hydration: drink ORS, coconut water, fresh juices, and water (at least 2.5 to 3 liters daily).
Take ONLY Paracetamol (500 mg or 650 mg) for fever and severe body pain. Do not exceed 3000 mg in 24 hours.
STRICTLY AVOID Ibuprofen, Aspirin, Diclofenac, or any NSAIDs, because they dramatically increase the risk of severe internal bleeding.
Monitor for warning signs every day (usually between day 3 to 7 as fever subsides): severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from nose/gums, or extreme lethargy.
Get daily blood tests (CBC / Platelet count) as directed by your physician to track platelet trends and hematocrit.

doctor_answer.assessment: Dengue Virus Infection (DENV 1-4). Classify per WHO: Dengue without Warning Signs, Dengue with Warning Signs, Severe Dengue (severe plasma leakage, severe hemorrhage, severe organ impairment).
doctor_answer.investigations: CBC with differential and hematocrit (Hct) daily. Dengue NS1 Antigen (days 1-5), Dengue IgM/IgG antibodies (day 5 onwards). LFTs and ultrasound abdomen (gallbladder wall edema, ascites, pleural effusion indicating plasma leakage).
doctor_answer.management: Judicious fluid management is the cornerstone of therapy. In Dengue with warning signs: IV isotonic crystalloids (0.9% Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate) at 5-7 mL/kg/h for 1-2 hours, titrated down according to hematocrit and urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/h). Platelet transfusion is NOT routinely recommended for low platelet counts alone unless there is significant active bleeding or platelets < 10,000/mcL.
references: WHO Guidelines for Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention & Control of Dengue (2020)
NVBDCP (National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, India) Dengue Guidelines

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Orange if warning signs present; Yellow if stable. Check BP, pulse pressure (narrow pulse pressure <= 20 mmHg indicates shock), hematocrit, and platelet count. Ensure accurate input-output charting.
red_flags: Severe continuous abdominal pain or tenderness
Persistent vomiting (>=3 episodes in 12 hours)
Mucosal bleeding: bleeding gums, epistaxis, black melena, or heavy menstrual bleeding
Cold, clammy extremities with rapid weak pulse (Dengue Shock Syndrome)
Sudden drop in platelets accompanied by sharp rise in hematocrit (>20%)
follow_up_questions: What day of fever are you currently on?
Are you able to drink and hold down liquids?
Have you noticed any bleeding from your gums, nose, or in your stool?
avoid: Do NOT take Ibuprofen, Brufen, Aspirin, or any pain injection (NSAIDs cause severe fatal bleeding in dengue)
Do NOT perform unnecessary prophylactic platelet transfusions without active bleeding
source: WHO Comprehensive Guidelines for Dengue & NVBDCP India

patient_answer: Seek medical evaluation immediately for a rapid blood test if you experience high fever with violent shivering and shaking chills.
Stay well-hydrated with clean water, ORS, and warm broths.
Take Paracetamol for fever spikes while waiting for diagnostic test results.
Take the full prescribed course of antimalarial medications without skipping doses, even after you start feeling better.
Prevent mosquito bites by sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets, using mosquito repellents, and wearing full-length clothing.

doctor_answer.assessment: Malaria (Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium falciparum). Screen immediately for signs of Severe Malaria: cerebral malaria (unconsciousness/seizures), severe anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL), acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, jaundice.
doctor_answer.investigations: Thick and thin peripheral blood smear (gold standard for species and parasite density) + Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) for Malaria (Pf HRP2 / Pan-pLDH). CBC, LFT, serum creatinine, blood glucose.
doctor_answer.management: Uncomplicated P. falciparum: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT: Artemether-Lumefantrine or Artesunate-SP) for 3 days + single dose Primaquine (0.25 mg/kg). Uncomplicated P. vivax: Chloroquine (25 mg/kg over 3 days) + Primaquine (0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days to prevent relapse; check G6PD status first). Severe Malaria: IV Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours, then daily.
references: WHO Guidelines for Malaria (2023)
NVBDCP National Drug Policy on Malaria (India)

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow (uncomplicated) or Red (altered sensorium/jaundice). Perform rapid malaria strip test immediately. Collect peripheral blood smear before initiating antimalarials if possible.
red_flags: Confusion, delirium, drowsiness, or convulsions (Cerebral Malaria)
Extreme breathlessness or deep acidotic breathing
Severe jaundice with dark yellow/tea-colored urine
Inability to retain oral medications due to intractable vomiting
follow_up_questions: Did the fever start with severe shaking chills followed by sweating?
Have you traveled to any forest or malaria-endemic regions recently?
Have you had a blood smear or rapid malaria test done yet?
avoid: Do NOT delay antimalarial therapy if test is positive
Do NOT administer Primaquine to patients with G6PD deficiency without specialist monitoring (causes severe hemolysis)
source: WHO Guidelines for Malaria & NVBDCP India

patient_answer: Drink ONLY boiled or commercially bottled purified water and consume freshly cooked, piping hot food.
Eat soft, easily digestible foods like khichdi, porridge, mashed potatoes, and curd.
Take Paracetamol for temperature control and drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.
Complete the entire course of prescribed antibiotics strictly as instructed by your doctor, even if the fever subsides.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the restroom and before eating to prevent spreading bacteria to family members.

doctor_answer.assessment: Enteric Fever (Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi or Paratyphi). Characterized by stepwise rising fever, relative bradycardia (Faget's sign), coated tongue, hepatosplenomegaly, and abdominal pain.
doctor_answer.investigations: Blood Culture (gold standard, highest sensitivity in week 1). CBC (look for leukopenia/anemia). Note: Widal test has low specificity and should not be used as sole diagnostic basis; paired titers showing 4-fold rise required.
doctor_answer.management: Uncomplicated enteric fever (outpatient): Oral Azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day (up to 1 g daily) for 7 days or Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day for 14 days (due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance). Severe / Inpatient: IV Ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 10-14 days. Monitor for 3rd-week complications: intestinal perforation and GI hemorrhage.
references: WHO Guidelines on the Management of Typhoid Fever
ICMR Antimicrobial Guidelines for Enteric Fever

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow. Collect blood culture before starting antibiotics. Screen for sudden abdominal guarding or peritonitis (sign of intestinal perforation). Maintain enteric precautions.
red_flags: Sudden severe sharp abdominal pain with rigid abdomen (Intestinal Perforation)
Black tarry stools or vomiting fresh blood (GI Hemorrhage)
High prolonged fever with extreme delirium, lethargy, or coma (Typhoid state)
follow_up_questions: How many days have you had this continuous fever?
Have you consumed untreated water, street food, or raw salads recently?
Have you had a blood culture test performed?
avoid: Do NOT stop antibiotics early when fever breaks (leads to chronic carrier state and relapse)
Do NOT rely blindly on a single baseline Widal test for definitive diagnosis
source: ICMR Antimicrobial Stewardship Guidelines & WHO Enteric Fever Protocols

patient_answer: Get plenty of rest and avoid strenuous weight-bearing activities during the acute painful phase.
Take Paracetamol (500 mg or 650 mg) every 6 hours for fever and joint discomfort.
Apply cold damp packs or gel ice wraps around swollen painful joints for 15 minutes to reduce inflammation.
Maintain high fluid intake with water, ORS, and warm soups.
Engage in gentle range-of-motion stretching once the acute fever has subsided to prevent joint stiffness.

doctor_answer.assessment: Chikungunya Virus Infection (Alphavirus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes). Triad of acute high fever, severe crippling polyarthralgia/polyarthritis (predominantly wrists, ankles, small joints of hands), and maculopapular rash.
doctor_answer.investigations: RT-PCR (days 1-7 of onset), Chikungunya IgM ELISA antibodies (day 5 onwards). CBC (rule out severe thrombocytopenia).
doctor_answer.management: Supportive therapy. Antipyretics: Paracetamol 1 g QID PRN. Once dengue is excluded and fever resolved: Short-course NSAIDs (Naproxen 500 mg BID or Celecoxib) for persistent arthralgia. Chronic arthropathy (>3 months): Consider hydroxychloroquine or low-dose methotrexate under rheumatology supervision.
references: WHO Guidelines for Chikungunya Management
CDC Clinical Guidance: Chikungunya Virus

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Green/Yellow. Provide comfortable seating and assist with mobility if patient has crippling hand/knee pain. Verify that dengue has been ruled out before any NSAID administration.
red_flags: Joints becoming hot, bright red, and purulent (secondary bacterial arthritis)
Neurological symptoms such as confusion, neck rigidity, or seizures (Chikungunya meningoencephalitis)
Severe dehydration or inability to walk safely
follow_up_questions: Which specific joints are hurting and are they visibly swollen?
Did you develop a red rash alongside the fever?
Has dengue been ruled out by your doctor?
avoid: Do NOT take NSAIDs (Brufen/Aspirin) during the initial acute febrile phase until Dengue is ruled out
Do NOT use systemic steroids in the acute viral phase
source: WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia Guidelines & CDC Chikungunya Guidance

patient_answer: Visit a public health center, DOTS clinic, or chest physician immediately for a free sputum test (CBNAAT / GeneXpert) if you have had a cough for more than 2 weeks.
Cover your mouth and nose with a handkerchief or wear a surgical mask whenever you cough or sneeze to protect your family.
Ensure your living spaces are well-ventilated with windows open to allow plenty of fresh air and sunlight.
Eat high-protein, calorie-rich meals (eggs, milk, lentils, nuts, beans) to rebuild weight and immune strength.
NEVER miss a dose or stop taking your anti-TB medications prematurely; incomplete treatment leads to dangerous Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB).

doctor_answer.assessment: Pulmonary Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis). Classical presentation: productive cough > 2 weeks, hemoptysis, low-grade evening fever, drenching night sweats, and significant anorexia/weight loss.
doctor_answer.investigations: Sputum for Rapid Molecular Diagnostic (CBNAAT / Truenat / GeneXpert MTB/RIF for TB detection and Rifampicin resistance). Chest Radiograph (CXR: apical cavitary or infiltrate lesions). Baseline CBC, LFTs, Serum Creatinine, and HIV screening.
doctor_answer.management: National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP) standard regimen for drug-sensitive TB: 2 months of HRZE (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) Intensive Phase followed by 4 months of HRE Continuation Phase (fixed-dose combinations dosed by weight band). Add Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6 10-25 mg daily) to prevent isoniazid neuropathy.
references: Central TB Division, MoHFW India: NTEP Guidelines for TB Care in India
WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis (2022)

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow / Infection Control. Immediately provide a triple-layer mask to the coughing patient. Direct to designated well-ventilated sputum collection area. Register patient on Ni-kshay portal.
red_flags: Massive hemoptysis (>100-200 mL of blood coughed up in 24 hours - Life Threatening)
Severe shortness of breath or sudden unilateral chest pain (Hydropneumothorax)
Jaundice, vomiting, or dark tea-colored urine while taking anti-TB drugs (Drug-Induced Liver Injury)
follow_up_questions: How many weeks have you been coughing?
Have you coughed up any blood or rusty colored sputum?
Have you noticed drenching night sweats or clothing becoming very loose?
avoid: NEVER take fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin/Levofloxacin) as empiric monotherapy for chronic cough (masks TB diagnosis and drives quinolone resistance)
Do NOT stop TB medications without physician consultation
source: National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP), MoHFW India & WHO TB Guidelines

patient_answer: Isolate yourself in a well-ventilated separate room and use a dedicated bathroom if possible.
Monitor your blood oxygen level (SpO2) using a pulse oximeter every 6 hours while resting.
Take Paracetamol for fever and body ache, and drink plenty of warm fluids (water, soups, ORS).
Practice proning (lying on your stomach with pillows under chest and hips) for 30 to 45 minutes to improve oxygen distribution in your lungs.
Seek immediate emergency care if your oxygen saturation drops below 94%, or if you develop chest pain or severe breathlessness.

doctor_answer.assessment: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 infection). Stratify severity: Mild (URTI symptoms without hypoxia), Moderate (SpO2 90-93% on room air, RR 24-30), Severe (SpO2 < 90%, RR > 30).
doctor_answer.investigations: Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) or RT-PCR. In moderate-severe disease: CBC (lymphopenia), CRP, Ferritin, D-dimer, Chest X-ray / HRCT Chest if worsening hypoxia.
doctor_answer.management: Mild (home isolation): Symptomatic care with Paracetamol, oral hydration. High risk for progression: Consider oral Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir (Paxlovid) within 5 days of onset. Moderate/Severe: Hospitalization, supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 92-96%, Systemic Corticosteroids (Dexamethasone 6 mg IV/oral daily for up to 10 days), prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). Do NOT use steroids in mild cases without hypoxia.
references: WHO Therapeutics and COVID-19 Living Guideline
ICMR National Clinical Management Protocol for COVID-19

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Orange if SpO2 < 94%; Green if SpO2 >= 95%. Verify pulse oximeter reading on a warm finger. Ensure patient wears N95 mask. Isolate in respiratory triage area.
red_flags: SpO2 dropping below 94% on room air at rest
Persistent pain or severe pressure in the chest
Inability to speak complete sentences without gasping
Confusion, blue-tinted lips, or altered level of consciousness
follow_up_questions: What is your current pulse oximeter SpO2 reading?
Do you have underlying conditions like diabetes, hypertension, or heart disease?
How many days has it been since symptoms started?
avoid: Do NOT take steroids (Dexamethasone, Prednisolone) in mild COVID-19 with normal oxygen levels (worsens viral replication and spikes blood sugar)
Do NOT take unnecessary antibiotics like Azithromycin for uncomplicated viral COVID-19
source: ICMR Clinical Guidance for Management of COVID-19 & WHO Therapeutics Guideline

topic: Seasonal Influenza / Flu (H1N1 / Influenza A & B)
patient_answer: Stay home and get plenty of rest to support your body's immune defense and prevent infecting coworkers or classmates.
Drink abundant fluids: warm broths, herbal teas, electrolyte solutions, and water.
Take Paracetamol for fever, headache, and severe body chills.
Use saline nasal spray and steam inhalation to ease nasal congestion.
High-risk individuals (pregnant women, elderly, diabetic, asthmatic) should see a doctor within 48 hours for antiviral medication.

doctor_answer.assessment: Acute Seasonal Influenza (Influenza A/B or pandemic H1N1). Sudden abrupt onset of high fever, severe myalgias, headache, dry cough, and prostration.
doctor_answer.investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab RT-PCR or rapid influenza molecular assay. CBC, CXR if suspected secondary bacterial pneumonia.
doctor_answer.management: Neuraminidase inhibitor: Oral Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) 75 mg BID for 5 days. Most effective when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset; indicated regardless of timing in hospitalized, severely ill, or high-risk patients. Bacterial co-infection (e.g. S. aureus, S. pneumoniae) requires appropriate antibiotics.
references: CDC Influenza Antiviral Medications: Summary for Clinicians
WHO Guidelines on Pharmacological Management of Pandemic Influenza

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow / Orange for high-risk individuals with tachypnea. Give surgical mask. Check SpO2 and lung sounds. Ask about annual flu vaccination.
red_flags: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Fever that improves and then returns worse with a productive cough (Secondary bacterial pneumonia)
Severe dizziness or confusion
Persistent vomiting with inability to drink fluids
follow_up_questions: Did the symptoms hit you abruptly like a truck within a few hours?
Are you pregnant, over 65, or do you have chronic asthma or diabetes?
How many hours or days ago did the symptoms begin?
avoid: NEVER give Aspirin to children or adolescents with flu-like illness (prevents Reye's Syndrome)
Do NOT take antibiotics unless secondary bacterial pneumonia is diagnosed
source: CDC Clinical Overview of Influenza & WHO Guidelines

topic: Acute Viral Hepatitis A & E (Feco-Oral Jaundice / Peeliya)
patient_answer: Get adequate bed rest while feeling fatigued; avoid strenuous physical exertion.
Eat small, frequent, high-carbohydrate, easily digestible meals (sugarcane juice from hygienic source, glucose, khichdi, boiled vegetables, fruits).
Drink only boiled or purified water; avoid all outside food, street snacks, and unpasteurized juices.
STRICTLY AVOID ALL ALCOHOL consumption, as alcohol directly damages inflamed liver cells.
Consult a doctor immediately if you experience extreme drowsiness, confusion, or continuous vomiting.

doctor_answer.assessment: Acute Viral Hepatitis (HAV or HEV). Feco-orally transmitted. Note: HEV infection carries high mortality (up to 20-25%) due to fulminant hepatic failure in pregnant women in the third trimester.
doctor_answer.investigations: Liver Function Tests (markedly elevated serum transaminases ALT/AST often >1000 U/L, elevated direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase), Viral Serology: Anti-HAV IgM, Anti-HEV IgM. Prothrombin Time / INR (essential indicator of acute liver failure).
doctor_answer.management: Supportive care. No specific antiviral required for acute HAV/HEV. Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (limit paracetamol to <=2 g/day; avoid sedatives). Monitor PT/INR and sensorium regularly for early signs of Fulminant Hepatic Failure (FHF).
references: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on Hepatitis A and E Virus Infection
AASLD Guidelines on Acute Liver Failure

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Orange if pregnant or showing flapping tremors/confusion; Yellow if stable jaundice. Check PT/INR and total bilirubin. Maintain strict enteric precautions.
red_flags: Extreme drowsiness, day-night sleep reversal, confusion, or flapping tremor of hands (Hepatic Encephalopathy)
INR > 1.5 indicating acute hepatic coagulopathy
Infection in a pregnant woman (critical emergency risk for HEV-induced acute liver failure)
Intractable vomiting and inability to maintain hydration
follow_up_questions: What color is your urine and are the whites of your eyes visibly yellow?
Are you currently pregnant?
Have you consumed unpurified water or street food in the last 2 to 6 weeks?
avoid: STRICTLY AVOID ALL ALCOHOL
Do NOT consume untested herbal concoctions or 'jaundice tonics' which frequently trigger fatal toxic hepatitis
source: European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) & WHO Hepatitis Fact Sheets

patient_answer: Consult a hepatologist or gastroenterologist for viral load testing (HBV DNA / HCV RNA) and liver fibrosis evaluation.
Hepatitis C is now completely curable in over 95% of patients with a 12-week course of oral antiviral tablets.
Hepatitis B can be highly effectively controlled with daily antiviral medication to protect your liver and prevent cirrhosis.
Do not share toothbrushes, razors, nail clippers, or needles, and practice protected intercourse to prevent transmitting the virus.
Get vaccinated against Hepatitis A to provide double protection for your liver, and completely abstain from alcohol.

doctor_answer.assessment: Chronic Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) or Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) infection. Assess for liver cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
doctor_answer.investigations: HBV: HBsAg, HBeAg/Anti-HBe, quantitative HBV DNA PCR. HCV: Anti-HCV, quantitative HCV RNA PCR, genotype if needed. Baseline: LFT, CBC (platelets for portal hypertension), PT/INR, Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP), abdominal ultrasound, Transient Elastography (FibroScan).
doctor_answer.management: Chronic HBV: Nucleos(t)ide analogues with high barrier to resistance (Tenofovir Alafenamide 25 mg or Entecavir 0.5 mg daily) if elevated HBV DNA and elevated ALT / evidence of fibrosis. Chronic HCV: Pan-genotypic Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAA: Sofosbuvir 400 mg + Velpatasvir 100 mg daily) for 12 weeks achieves >95% SVR (cure).
references: AASLD-IDSA Guidance: Hepatitis C: Guidance for Testing, Managing, and Treating
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on Hepatitis B

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Green unless ascites, hematemesis, or jaundice present. Screen family members and close sexual contacts of HBV positive patients for HBsAg and Hepatitis B vaccination.
red_flags: Vomiting blood or black stools (Bleeding Esophageal Varices)
Swelling of the abdomen with fluid (Ascites)
Yellow discoloration of eyes with sudden confusion
Weight loss and right upper quadrant abdominal lump
follow_up_questions: Have you had a quantitative viral load test (HBV DNA or HCV RNA)?
Have you ever had an ultrasound or FibroScan of your liver?
Has your doctor screened you for Hepatitis B vaccination status among household members?
avoid: Do NOT drink alcohol in any quantity (accelerates cirrhosis and liver cancer development)
Do NOT share razors, nail cutters, or piercing equipment
source: AASLD / EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines & National Viral Hepatitis Control Program (NVHCP) India

patient_answer: Call 112 or get to an emergency hospital immediately; cholera can cause fatal dehydration within hours.
Start drinking WHO-standard Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution continuously on the way to the medical center.
Drink 1 glass of ORS every few minutes; do not wait to feel thirsty.
Do NOT drink unboiled tap water, well water, or contaminated river water.
Maintain strict hand washing with soap to prevent spreading the infection to other members of the household.

doctor_answer.assessment: Cholera (Vibrio cholerae O1 / O139). Clinical hallmark: Sudden painless onset of profuse, watery 'rice-water' stools with fishy odor, rapid hypovolemic shock, and severe metabolic acidosis.
doctor_answer.investigations: Stool darkfield microscopy (darting motility), rapid cholera dipstick, stool culture on TCBS medium. Serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, arterial blood gas.
doctor_answer.management: Immediate aggressive fluid resuscitation (Plan C): IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg (30 mL/kg in first 30 min, then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours in adults; slower in infants). Transition to WHO ORS once awake and drinking. Antibiotics (shorten duration and excretion): Single dose oral Doxycycline 300 mg or Azithromycin 1 g oral. Zinc supplementation in children.
references: WHO Technical Guidance: Cholera Outbreak: Assessing the Outbreak Response and Improving Preparedness
CDC Recommendations for Cholera Treatment

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Red. Immediately insert two large-bore IV cannulas (16G or 18G) and hang Ringer's Lactate rapidly. Use cholera beds with a central hole and bucket to measure exact stool fluid loss. Report immediately to district surveillance.
red_flags: Severe dehydration: unrecordable blood pressure, thready pulse, wrinkled washerwoman's hands, sunken eyes
Severe muscle cramps caused by extreme potassium and sodium loss
Anuria (complete lack of urine output)
follow_up_questions: What does the stool look like (is it cloudy white like rice water)?
How many large volume stools have occurred in the last few hours?
Is the patient able to drink fluids?
avoid: Do NOT delay IV fluid resuscitation for lab results
Do NOT administer plain 5% Dextrose alone (does not correct severe electrolyte and volume depletion)
source: WHO Cholera Guidelines & CDC Global Health Protocols

patient_answer: Drink WHO-standard ORS solution in small, frequent sips to replace water and vital minerals lost from vomiting and diarrhea.
Eat simple, bland foods like steamed rice, plain toast, bananas, and light khichdi once vomiting pauses.
Do not take antimotility medicines (like Loperamide) if you have high fever or visible blood in the stool, as this traps bacterial toxins in the intestines.
Rest adequately and allow your digestive tract time to recover.
Seek medical attention if fever exceeds 38.5°C (101.3°F), if you notice blood in your stools, or if you cannot keep liquids down.

doctor_answer.assessment: Bacterial Gastroenteritis / Foodborne Illness. Common culprits: Preformed enterotoxin (S. aureus, B. cereus - rapid onset 1-6 hours with vomiting), Invasive/cytotoxic bacteria (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli STEC - onset 12-72h with fever and bloody stools).
doctor_answer.investigations: Stool routine and microscopy for fecal leukocytes, RBCs, and parasites. Stool culture if severe illness, dysentery, or persistent symptoms.
doctor_answer.management: Hydration therapy (oral ORS or IV Ringer's Lactate). Antimicrobial therapy indicated for severe illness or documented invasive pathogens: Oral Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID for 3 days or Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days. Avoid fluoroquinolones if Campylobacter suspected; avoid antibiotics in suspected E. coli O157:H7 (STEC) due to increased risk of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
references: IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea
ACG Clinical Guideline on Acute Diarrhea

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow. Check hydration status, vitals, and ask if multiple family members who shared the same meal became ill at the same time.
red_flags: Stool containing visible red blood or pus (Dysentery)
High spiking fever (> 38.5°C / 101.3°F)
Severe postural lightheadedness or syncope
Signs of kidney impairment: dark urine or sudden drop in urine volume (concern for HUS)
follow_up_questions: Did anyone else who ate the same food become ill?
How many hours after eating did the symptoms start?
Are there streaks of blood in the stool?
avoid: Do NOT take Loperamide (Imodium) if fever or bloody diarrhea is present
Do NOT give antibiotics empirically if E. coli O157 / STEC is suspected
source: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Diarrheal Guidelines

patient_answer: Drink 2 to 3 liters of water daily to frequently flush bacteria out of your bladder.
Do not postpone urination; empty your bladder completely whenever you feel the urge and after sexual intercourse.
Apply a warm heating pad to your lower abdomen to relieve bladder cramping.
Wipe from front to back after using the toilet to avoid introducing bacteria from the rectum into the urethra.
See a doctor to get a urine test and receive targeted prescription antibiotics; avoid self-medicating with leftover pills.

doctor_answer.assessment: Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis (Lower UTI) vs Complicated UTI (males, pregnancy, diabetes, anatomical abnormalities, indwelling catheter) vs Acute Pyelonephritis (upper UTI). Most common pathogen: uropathogenic E. coli (75-90%).
doctor_answer.investigations: Urine Routine and Microscopy (pyuria >=10 WBCs/hpf, bacteriuria, positive nitrites/leukocyte esterase). Urine Culture and Antibiotic Sensitivity testing mandatory in complicated, recurrent, or treatment-failure cases.
doctor_answer.management: First-line uncomplicated cystitis: Oral Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID for 5 days, or Fosfomycin Trometamol 3 g single-dose oral sachet. Alternative: Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg BID for 3 days (if local resistance <20%). Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin/Levofloxacin) should be reserved for pyelonephritis or complicated UTI due to collateral damage.
references: IDSA Guidelines for the Treatment of Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis and Pyelonephritis
EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections (2023)

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Green unless high fever with flank tenderness (Pyelonephritis - Triage Yellow). Instruct patient on proper midstream clean-catch urine specimen collection.
red_flags: High fever, chills, and one-sided flank or lower back pain (Acute Pyelonephritis)
Visible frank blood in urine (Gross Hematuria)
Inability to pass urine with painful palpable bladder (Urinary Retention)
UTI symptoms during pregnancy (requires urgent treatment to prevent preterm labor)
follow_up_questions: Do you have back or side pain, fever, or chills?
Are you pregnant?
Have you had frequent bladder infections before?
avoid: Do NOT take arbitrary over-the-counter antibiotics without a urine test
Do NOT delay medical care if experiencing fever or flank pain
source: European Association of Urology (EAU) & IDSA Guidelines

patient_answer: Seek medical attention promptly if you have a fever accompanied by a productive cough (yellow or green phlegm), chest pain when breathing, and shortness of breath.
Rest in bed and stay well-hydrated with warm fluids to loosen sticky mucus.
Take Paracetamol for fever and chest discomfort as advised by your doctor.
Use a pulse oximeter to check your oxygen saturation (SpO2); if it dips below 94%, go to the emergency room immediately.
Complete the full course of prescribed antibiotics exactly as instructed without stopping early.

doctor_answer.assessment: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP). Common pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, atypical agents (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella). Risk-stratify using CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea > 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >= 30, BP SBP < 90 or DBP <= 60, Age >= 65).
doctor_answer.investigations: Chest Radiograph (PA view: lobar consolidation or patchy infiltrates). CBC, CRP, Sputum Gram stain and culture, Blood cultures (in hospitalized patients), pulse oximetry, ABG if hypoxic.
doctor_answer.management: Outpatient (CURB-65 0-1): Amoxicillin-Clavulanate 1 g BID (or Amoxicillin 1 g TID) + Macrolide (Azithromycin 500 mg daily) or Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 5-7 days. Inpatient (CURB-65 >= 2): IV Ceftriaxone 1-2 g daily + IV Azithromycin 500 mg daily. Supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 94-98% (88-92% in hypercapnic COPD).
references: ATS/IDSA Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-Acquired Pneumonia
BTS Clinical Guidelines for the Management of CAP in Adults

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Orange if SpO2 < 94% or RR >= 25/min; Yellow if stable. Check pulse oximeter, blood pressure, and mental orientation. Obtain CXR and sputum sample.
red_flags: SpO2 < 92% on room air
Respiratory rate > 30 breaths/min
Confusion, disorientation, or drowsiness (especially in elderly patients)
Systolic BP < 90 mmHg (Septic Shock)
Coughing up significant amounts of blood
follow_up_questions: What is your current oxygen reading (SpO2)?
Does it hurt sharply in your chest when you take a deep breath?
What color is the phlegm you are coughing up?
avoid: Do NOT suppress productive cough with strong antitussive syrups (clearing secretions is vital)
Do NOT delay medical evaluation when breathing difficulty accompanies a cough
source: American Thoracic Society (ATS) / IDSA Guidelines & British Thoracic Society (BTS)

patient_answer: Isolate the sick child or adult immediately; measles is one of the most highly contagious airborne viral diseases known.
Keep the patient comfortable in a dimly lit room, as bright light often causes uncomfortable eye sensitivity (photophobia).
Encourage frequent sips of liquids (water, ORS, breast milk for infants) to prevent dehydration.
Give Paracetamol for fever relief. NEVER give Aspirin to children.
Consult a doctor to administer Vitamin A supplements, which are crucial to reduce complications and protect eyesight in measles.

doctor_answer.assessment: Measles (Morbillivirus infection). Classical prodrome (3 C's: Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis) with high fever, followed by pathognomonic Koplik spots (white tiny grain-like spots on buccal mucosa opposite molars), then a maculopapular blanching rash spreading cephalocaudally (hairline downwards).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Confirmation via Measles IgM serology or throat/nasopharyngeal swab for RT-PCR. Notify public health authorities.
doctor_answer.management: Supportive care and isolation. WHO standard Vitamin A supplementation: 200,000 IU orally daily for 2 days for children >=12 months (100,000 IU for 6-11 months, 50,000 IU for <6 months) to prevent blindness and decrease mortality. Treat secondary bacterial complications (otitis media, pneumonia) with antibiotics.
references: WHO Measles Fact Sheet & Guidelines for Epidemic Preparedness and Response
CDC Clinical Guidance: Measles (Rubeola)

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Orange / Strict Airborne Isolation. Place in negative pressure isolation room if available. Healthcare staff must wear N95 respirators. Notify infection control team.
red_flags: Rapid breathing, chest indrawing, or grunting (Pneumonia - leading cause of measles death)
Convulsions, extreme drowsiness, or neck stiffness (Measles Encephalitis)
Severe diarrhea leading to dehydration
Corneal ulceration or cloudiness (Vitamin A deficiency complication)
follow_up_questions: Has the person received the MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) vaccine?
Did the rash start along the hairline and behind the ears before moving down the body?
Are there small white salt-like spots inside the cheeks?
avoid: NEVER give Aspirin to children (risk of fatal Reye's Syndrome)
Do NOT expose unvaccinated individuals or pregnant women to the patient
source: WHO Guidelines on Measles Management & CDC Clinical Overview

patient_answer: Apply calamine lotion to the itchy fluid-filled blisters to soothe irritation and speed drying.
Take lukewarm baths with baking soda or colloidal oatmeal to relieve intense itching.
Keep fingernails short and clean to prevent scratching, which causes scarring and secondary bacterial skin infections.
Take Paracetamol for fever; NEVER give Aspirin or Ibuprofen to children with chickenpox.
Isolate at home until all blisters have completely dried and formed crusty scabs (usually 5 to 7 days).

doctor_answer.assessment: Varicella (Chickenpox: generalized pruritic vesicular rash in various stages of healing - 'dewdrops on rose petal') vs Herpes Zoster (Shingles: dermatomal, painful, unilateral vesicular eruption).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. PCR for VZV DNA from vesicle fluid or Tzanck smear if atypical or immunocompromised.
doctor_answer.management: Uncomplicated pediatric varicella: Symptomatic care (oral antihistamines, calamine). Avoid Ibuprofen (associated with severe invasive Group A Streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis). High-risk varicella (adults, immunocompromised, pregnant) or Herpes Zoster: Oral Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days (or Valacyclovir 1000 mg TID for 7 days) initiated within 72 hours of rash onset.
references: CDC Clinical Guidance: Chickenpox (Varicella) & Shingles (Herpes Zoster)
NICE CKS: Chickenpox & Shingles

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow / Contact and Airborne precautions. Isolate patient from pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals. Ensure all scabs are crusted before clearing for school/work.
red_flags: Skin around the blisters becoming swollen, red, hot, and exquisitely tender (Secondary bacterial cellulitis)
Breathlessness, persistent cough, or chest pain (Varicella Pneumonia)
Unsteadiness, stumbling gait, or confusion (Varicella Cerebellar Ataxia)
Blisters appearing near or in the eye (Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus - urgent eye risk)
follow_up_questions: Are all the blisters crusted over or are new fluid-filled bumps still appearing?
Is the rash on both sides of the body or strictly along a single band on one side?
Have you had the chickenpox vaccine?
avoid: NEVER give Aspirin (risk of Reye's Syndrome)
AVOID Ibuprofen (Brufen) during chickenpox due to increased risk of severe necrotizing skin infections
Do NOT scratch the scabs
source: CDC Varicella Guidelines & American Academy of Pediatrics

patient_answer: IMMEDIATELY wash the bite or scratch wound thoroughly under running tap water with soap for at least 15 continuous minutes. This single step removes up to 80% of the virus.
Apply an antiseptic like povidone-iodine (Betadine) or 70% alcohol to the wound after washing.
Proceed directly to the nearest hospital or anti-rabies vaccination clinic immediately.
Do NOT apply chili powder, lime, turmeric, mud, or herbal pastes to the wound.
Do NOT bandage, wrap tightly, or suture the wound unless absolutely necessary for severe bleeding.
Complete all doses of the modern Anti-Rabies Vaccine (ARV) on schedule (Days 0, 3, 7, and 28).

doctor_answer.assessment: Animal Bite Exposure for Rabies. Classify WHO Exposure Category: Category I (touching/feeding animals, licks on intact skin - No PEP), Category II (minor scratches/abrasions without bleeding - ARV immediately), Category III (transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin, mucous membrane contamination, or bat exposures - ARV + Rabies Immunoglobulin).
doctor_answer.investigations: No lab test needed for PEP decision; start prophylaxis immediately without waiting for animal quarantine.
doctor_answer.management: Wound washing for >=15 min with soap and water. Category III: Infiltrate Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG: Human RIG 20 IU/kg or Equine RIG 40 IU/kg) into and around all wound sites; remaining volume IM. Modern Rabies Cell-Culture Vaccine (ARV: 0.5 mL IM in deltoid or intradermal Essen/Thai regimen) on Days 0, 3, 7, and 28. Administer Tetanus Toxoid booster if due. Strictly avoid suturing wounds; if unavoidable, loosely suture only after RIG infiltration.
references: WHO Expert Consultation on Rabies (Third Report) & WHO Position Paper on Rabies Vaccines (2018)
National Guidelines for Rabies Prophylaxis, MoHFW India

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Red/Orange. Escort immediately to clean running water tap and scrub wound with soap and water for 15 minutes. Check Category III status (bleeding wound = needs RIG). Prepare ARV injection and calculate RIG dose based on patient's exact body weight.
red_flags: Deep puncture wounds with bleeding (Category III requiring RIG)
Bites located near the head, neck, face, or hands (short incubation route to brain)
Wild animal or stray dog that was unprovoked and displaying aggressive or erratic behavior
Rabies clinical onset (hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation - almost 100% fatal once clinical symptoms begin)
follow_up_questions: Did the bite or scratch break the skin and bleed?
Has the wound been washed with soap under running water for 15 minutes?
Is the animal a pet that can be observed for 10 days, or a stray/wild animal?
avoid: Do NOT apply turmeric, chilies, lime, or kerosene to bite wounds
Do NOT suture fresh animal bite wounds primarily
Do NOT delay vaccination while attempting to observe a stray animal
source: WHO Rabies Vaccines Position Paper & National Center for Disease Control (NCDC) India

patient_answer: Seek immediate medical evaluation for acute fever if you have recently walked through brush, vegetation, or rural farmland.
Check your skin carefully (especially groin, armpits, waist, and behind ears) for a painless dark scab or cigarette-burn mark called an 'eschar'.
Take Paracetamol for fever while consulting a physician.
Take the full prescribed course of Doxycycline antibiotic as directed by your doctor.
Wear protective clothing, tuck pants into socks, and apply DEET insect repellent when working in grassy fields.

doctor_answer.assessment: Scrub Typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by larval trombiculid mites/chiggers). Acute febrile illness with headache, myalgia, lymphadenopathy, and pathognomonic 'eschar' (punched-out ulcer with black necrotic crust, present in 40-70% of cases). Complications: ARDS, hepatitis, acute kidney injury, myocarditis.
doctor_answer.investigations: Thorough skin examination in good lighting for eschar. Scrub Typhus IgM ELISA (gold standard serology), Weil-Felix test (OX-K agglutination, low sensitivity). CBC (thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis), LFTs, creatinine, CXR.
doctor_answer.management: First-line: Oral Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days (dramatic defervescence typically within 24-48 hours confirms clinical diagnosis). Alternative (pregnant women and young children): Oral Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days. In severe cases with organ dysfunction: IV Doxycycline or IV Azithromycin.
references: ICMR Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Rickettsial Diseases in India
CDC Clinical Overview: Scrub Typhus

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow / Orange. Perform a whole-body skin exam in private cubicle looking specifically in axillae, groin, and neck folds for a characteristic black eschar.
red_flags: Difficulty breathing or rapid respiratory rate (Scrub typhus ARDS)
Oliguria or rising creatinine (Acute Kidney Injury)
Altered sensorium or delirium (Scrub Typhus Meningoencephalitis)
Hypotension and signs of septic shock
follow_up_questions: Have you visited rural fields, bushes, or farms recently?
Have you noticed any black scab-like mark on your skin that doesn't hurt or itch?
Has the fever lasted more than 5 days?
avoid: Do NOT delay Doxycycline treatment while waiting for confirmatory serology in endemic areas
Do NOT pick or scratch off the eschar scab
source: ICMR Guidelines for Rickettsial Diseases & CDC Scrub Typhus Protocols

patient_answer: Seek medical evaluation immediately if you experience high fever with severe calf muscle pain after walking through floodwaters or waterlogged streets.
Drink plenty of water and ORS to maintain kidney hydration.
Take Paracetamol for fever and pain.
Complete the prescribed antibiotic treatment without interruption.
Avoid wading through stagnant rainwater or floodwaters, especially if you have cuts or scrapes on your feet; wear protective gumboots.

doctor_answer.assessment: Leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans, transmitted via water contaminated with rodent urine). Biphasic illness: Anicteric leptospirosis (fever, intense conjunctival suffusion without purulence, severe calf tenderness) vs Icteric leptospirosis / Weil's Disease (triad of jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhagic diathesis).
doctor_answer.investigations: Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT, gold standard), Leptospira IgM ELISA. CBC (leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia), Serum Creatinine/BUN (renal failure), LFT (elevated bilirubin with mild-moderate transaminasemia), CPK, Urine routine (proteinuria, hematuria).
doctor_answer.management: Mild/outpatient: Oral Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days or Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 7 days. Severe/Weil's Disease: IV Crystalline Penicillin G 1.5 million units IV Q6H or IV Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily for 7 days. Supportive: Hemodialysis for acute renal failure; lung protective ventilation for pulmonary hemorrhage.
references: WHO Human Leptospirosis: Guidance for Detection and Control
MoHFW National Guidelines on Leptospirosis, India

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Orange if jaundice, oliguria, or hemoptysis present. Inspect eyes for red conjunctival suffusion without discharge and palpate gastrocnemius (calves) for exquisite tenderness.
red_flags: Severe jaundice with rapidly rising creatinine and low urine output (Weil's Disease)
Coughing up fresh blood or acute breathlessness (Severe Pulmonary Hemorrhagic Syndrome - High Mortality)
Cardiac arrhythmias or profound hypotension
follow_up_questions: Did you wade through rainwater, floods, or muddy water with bare feet?
Do you have red eyes and severe tenderness in your calf muscles?
Have you noticed your urine becoming very dark or decreasing in amount?
avoid: Do NOT walk barefoot in stagnant water or flood puddles
Do NOT delay hospital admission if jaundice or oliguria occurs after flood exposure
source: WHO Guidelines on Leptospirosis & MoHFW India Protocols

patient_answer: Drink plenty of safe, boiled or bottled water and WHO-standard ORS solution to prevent dehydration.
Eat simple, bland, soft meals like curd rice, boiled potatoes, and bananas.
Consult a doctor to have your stool examined under a microscope and get targeted anti-parasitic treatment.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before preparing food, eating, and after every restroom visit.
STRICTLY AVOID ALCOHOL during treatment with Metronidazole; combining them causes severe vomiting, flushing, and violent headache.

doctor_answer.assessment: Amoebic Dysentery (Invasive intestinal amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica). Symptoms: gradual onset of lower abdominal cramping, tenesmus, and frequent loose stools with red blood and mucus ('raspberry jam' appearance). Risk of Amoebic Liver Abscess.
doctor_answer.investigations: Fresh warm stool wet mount microscopy (identifying E. histolytica trophozoites with ingested RBCs - erythrophagocytosis). Stool E. histolytica antigen detection ELISA (differentiates from non-pathogenic E. dispar). Abdominal ultrasound to rule out amoebic liver abscess if right upper quadrant pain or fever.
doctor_answer.management: Two-step regimen: 1. Tissue amoebicide: Oral Metronidazole 400-800 mg TID for 7-10 days (or Tinidazole 2 g once daily for 3-5 days). 2. Luminal amoebicide (mandatory to eradicate cysts and prevent recurrence): Oral Paromomycin 25-35 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 7 days, or Diloxanide Furoate 500 mg TID for 10 days.
references: CDC Parasites - Amebiasis: Resources for Health Professionals
WHO Guidelines for the Control of Amoebiasis

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow. Check stool appearance for blood and mucus. Remind patient of strict alcohol avoidance with metronidazole.
red_flags: Severe right upper quadrant pain with high fever and shaking chills (Amoebic Liver Abscess)
Peritoneal signs: rigid abdomen or rebound tenderness (Toxic megacolon / colonic perforation)
Signs of severe dehydration with dizziness
follow_up_questions: Is there visible blood and jelly-like mucus in your stools?
Do you feel a painful, urgent need to pass stool even when bowel is empty (tenesmus)?
Do you have any pain in the upper right side of your belly?
avoid: STRICTLY AVOID ALCOHOL while taking Metronidazole or Tinidazole (triggers severe disulfiram reaction)
Do NOT take antimotility medicines (Loperamide) in dysentery
source: CDC Amebiasis Treatment Guidelines & WHO Treatment of Amoebiasis

patient_answer: Apply 5% Permethrin dermal cream over your entire body from the neck down to the tips of your toes, ensuring complete coverage between fingers, under fingernails, groin, and soles of feet.
Leave the cream on for 8 to 14 hours (usually overnight) before washing it off in a lukewarm bath.
Repeat the Permethrin application exactly 7 days later to kill newly hatched mites.
ALL household members, bedmates, and close contacts MUST be treated simultaneously, even if they currently do not have itching.
Wash all clothing, bedsheets, blankets, and towels used in the past 4 days in hot water (at least 50°C / 122°F) and dry on high heat, or seal in a plastic bag for 72 hours.

doctor_answer.assessment: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis ectoparasitic infestation). Hallmarks: Intense nocturnal pruritus, serpiginous burrows, erythematous papules in web spaces of fingers, wrists, axillae, umbilicus, and genitalia. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunocompromised.
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Definitive: Dermoscopy ('delta-wing jet' sign) or skin scraping with mineral oil under light microscopy demonstrating mites, eggs, or fecal pellets (scybala).
doctor_answer.management: First-line: Topical Permethrin 5% cream applied from jawline to soles, left on for 8-14 hours, repeated after 7 days. Oral Ivermectin (200 mcg/kg single oral dose with food, repeated on day 8 or 14) for institutional outbreaks, crusted scabies, or topical failures. Oral antihistamines (Cetirizine 10 mg) and mild topical corticosteroid for post-scabetic pruritus (which may persist for 2-4 weeks after successful mite eradication).
references: CDC Scabies Clinical Guidance & Treatment
IUSTI European Guideline for the Management of Scabies (2020)

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Green. Emphasize to the patient that every person living in the household must apply the cream on the exact same evening, otherwise reinfection will continually recur.
red_flags: Severe crusting, thick warty scaling over palms, soles, and trunk without typical itching (Crusted Scabies - millions of mites, highly infectious)
Extensive honey-colored crusts or pus on scratching areas (Secondary bacterial impetigo / Staphylococcal infection)
follow_up_questions: Is the itching dramatically worse at night when you get warm in bed?
Do other members of your family or roommates also have itching?
Do you have bumps or tracks between your fingers or around your wrists?
avoid: Do NOT treat only the symptomatic individual while ignoring household contacts (causes immediate reinfection)
Do NOT stop washing bedsheets in hot water
source: CDC Scabies Guidelines & International Alliance for the Control of Scabies (IACS)
